newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. envoy says Swiss must win support for fund.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy says Swiss must win support for fund.

text.p: The U.S. ambassador to Switzerland said on Thursday the Swiss government must do more to win popular support for a planned "solidarity foundation" to help the country deal with its World War Two past.

"The Swiss government must exert itself to explain the idea of the fund. In the U.S., one would say, 'a good idea deserves to be sold well'," ambassador Madeleine Kunin said in an interview in the Swiss daily newspaper Tages-Anzeiger.

Kunin declined to speculate on what would happen if the Swiss failed to approve the planned seven billion Swiss franc ($4.6 billion) fund. The fund would be set up to provide charity to both domestic and foreign causes.

The fund, which would pay out around 350 million francs annually based on calculations of its returns, was proposed by the government, now under international pressure to clarify the country's role during the Holocaust as a neutral neighbour of Nazi Germany.
Final approval will have to wait for a national referendum sometime in mid- or late 1998 under the country's system of direct democracy.

Rightwing leader Christoph Blocher, an industrialist and politician from one of the four government coalition parties, has pledged to oppose the fund becuase he says it is an admission of Swiss guilt.
He is proposing a privately-funded alternative foundation that would depend on donations from 400 wealthy Swiss, including himself.
Kunin also said the Swiss political process, which typically seeks a grassroots consensus before changes are adopted, may have slowed the country's response to the Holocaust.

"It (the structure of the political system) is certainly not very appropriate for dealing with crises, including international crises," she said. Such consensus-building also hindered anyone taking ultimate responsibility.

She also added that the Swiss reaction to the criticism of the country's wartime role had changed dramatically; a year ago there was doubt whether the issue of the unclaimed Holocaust bank accounts was even a topic.
"The government speaks very differently today," she said.
Kunin was appointed Swiss ambassador in August 1996.

The U.S. ambassador's mother was among those named on a list of nearly 1,800 dormant account holders which Swiss banks published on July 23. The banks published the list of names, from accounts set up during the war period when many Jews and other victims of Nazi Germany sought to secure their assets by placing them with Swiss banks.
Kunin said she was quite shocked when she learned her mother's name was on the list.
Kunin's emigrated to the US from Switzerland in 1940, fearing a Nazi invasion. Kunin has said earlier that her mother, Renee May, had not been a Holocaust victim.

"Up to now, the question of the dormant accounts was, for me, an official problem. Now I am personally affected. Am I biased because of this? I don't think so. This topic for all involved a very emotional one -- also for the Swiss," Kunin said. ($ = 1.513 Swiss Francs)
